contentBlocks.body: TypeScript has two ways to describe a fixed set of named values. An enum is a TypeScript-only construct that also produces a JavaScript object at runtime. A union of string literals is pure type information, erased at compile time, and the values are plain strings.

Numeric enums have extra surprises. Members without initializers are numbered from 0, and the compiler generates a reverse mapping, so Object.keys on a numeric enum returns both names and numbers. Numeric enums have also historically accepted arbitrary numbers where the enum type was expected.

contentBlocks.code:
enum Direction { Up, Down }        // Up = 0, Down = 1
Direction[0];                      // "Up" -- reverse mapping
Object.keys(Direction);            // ["0", "1", "Up", "Down"]

contentBlocks.body: When you also need the values at runtime (to validate input, render a dropdown, or loop), define them once as an as const array or object and derive the union type from it. You get one source of truth, no special emit, and an easy type guard.

Many teams default to literal unions plus as const. Newer TypeScript options such as erasableSyntaxOnly and Node's built-in type stripping reject enums outright, because enums are not just erasable type annotations: they generate code.
const enum is inlined at compile time and needs whole-program information, so it does not work under isolatedModules (which most bundlers and this project use).

knowledgeItems.prompt: Which of these produces a JavaScript object at runtime?

payload.explanation: Enums emit code. Type aliases, interfaces, and declare statements are erased.

knowledgeItems.prompt: For enum Direction { Up, Down }, what is Direction[1]?

payload.explanation: Numeric enums get a reverse mapping from value back to name.
